title: Supply concentration, export restrictions and declining investment put critical mineral security at risk (Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 news release)
date_evidence: News. 16 July 2026. Latest IEA analysis identifies widening range of vulnerabilities, though policy action – including on rare earths – shows progress is possible
key_claim: Critical-minerals investment fell 9% in 2025; the top refiners accounted for over three-quarters of refined-supply growth over two years; diversification investment concentrates in mining while refining and downstream capacity lag.
frame_summary: The IEA argues supply-chain risk is widening because refining concentration keeps rising and diversification pipelines are structurally imbalanced toward mining, even as public finance for minerals quadruples.
verbatim_quote: Price volatility and geopolitical tensions have weighed on investment, which fell by 9% in 2025, ending several consecutive years of growth.
verbatim_list: In rare earth supply chains, this means that planned refining capacity reaches only around two-thirds of expected mine output by 2035, while planned magnet production amounts to just one-third.
Public finance commitments more than quadrupled between 2023 and 2025, reaching $65 billion.

While many projects are being announced and developed across the globe, analysis of project pipelines outside the dominant supplier reveals a structural imbalance in supply chain diversification efforts – with investment concentrated in mining, while efforts to expand refining and downstream capacity lag behind.

title: Copper prices have hit record highs, but smelters face mounting strategic pressures (commentary)
key_claim: The annual copper TC/RC benchmark settled at USD 0 per tonne in January 2026, the lowest ever; China holds half of global smelting after taking over 90% of growth since 2005, and persistent low fees threaten custom smelters outside China with the nickel-style concentration pattern.
frame_summary: The IEA argues the copper midstream, not the mine, is where strategic risk is accumulating: Chinese smelter overcapacity has destroyed processing fees, by-product income is a fragile buffer, and without intervention copper could repeat nickel's concentration spiral.
verbatim_quote: The annual TC/RC benchmark, which is based on an agreement between Chilean miner Antofagasta and major Chinese smelters, settled at USD 0 per tonne in January 2026, the lowest level ever agreed in annual negotiations.
verbatim_list: Since 2005, China has accounted for over 90% of growth in global copper smelter output, lifting its share from around 15% to half of global supply in 2025.

China is the top refiner for 19 out of 20 strategic minerals that are critical for sectors including energy, defence, transport, aerospace, semiconductors and AI, with an average market share of around 70%.
Based on the current project pipeline, the IEA anticipates that the copper market could face a supply deficit of 30% by 2035.
However, these cuts are not enough to meaningfully balance the market.
China’s top smelters have agreed to cut production by over 10% in 2026, and the government has halted around 2 million tonnes of planned new smelting capacity to address the issue.

title: Protecting Existing US and Allied Copper Smelting Capacity
key_claim: Record-low TC/RCs put US and allied copper smelters at risk of closure even as copper demand is estimated to grow 50 percent from 2025 to 2040; once a smelter closes, restarting or replacing it costs billions and takes years.
frame_summary: CGEP argues allied governments should intervene now, with tools such as capacity support, modernization grants and tax credits, because losing existing smelters is far more expensive than keeping them and reinforces China's supply-chain control.
verbatim_quote: This has put copper smelters in the United States and allied economies—including the EU, Australia, Japan, Canada, and South Korea—at risk of closure, even as copper demand is estimated to increase by 50 percent from 2025 to 2040.
verbatim_list: China accounted for only about 8 percent of copper concentrate production, though it produced 48 percent of smelting output and exerts influence through investments in overseas projects.
China accounted for approximately 50 percent of copper smelter production in 2025 and has 12 of the 20 largest smelters by capacity.

title: Closing the Midstream Gap in India's Critical Minerals Strategy
key_claim: India's critical-minerals policy stack covers nearly every link except midstream separation, refining and metallisation, the stages where most value sits and where Chinese IP is most entrenched.
frame_summary: ORF argues that control of the midstream matters more than access to the resource, and that India's mine-and-stockpile policy stack will not deliver strategic autonomy until refining and metallisation move onshore with dedicated incentives.
verbatim_quote: India's gap lies in the midstream: the separation, refining, and metallurgy needed to transform mined ore into the high-purity oxides, alloys, and magnets that industry requires.
verbatim_list: China's grip on mineral processing underscores a broader truth: control over the midstream can be more consequential than access to the resource itself.
notes: Indian flagship think-tank perspective showing the midstream gap is a global pattern, not only a Western one. title: Key developments zinc concentrate participants are watching, from record Kipushi output to Korea smelter fire
key_claim: Spot zinc concentrate treatment charges sat at minus $70 to minus $120 per tonne in late June 2026, with smelters effectively paying miners for feed; some Chinese smelters trimmed run rates 5-10%.
frame_summary: Fastmarkets' price reporting shows the negative-treatment-charge squeeze extends beyond copper into zinc, with smelters worldwide competing for scarce concentrate and absorbing losses to keep running.
verbatim_quote: Negative TCs mean smelters effectively pay miners to secure concentrate, the inverse of the market’s normal structure, squeezing processor margins as competition for feed intensifies.

title: Column: Copper price soars but smelters can't bank on it to survive (Andy Home, Reuters)
key_claim: The copper TC/RC benchmark fell from $80/t in 2024 to $21.25 in 2025 to zero in 2026; China's refined output rose 8% to 14.72 million tonnes in 2025 against 1% global mine growth, and output kept rising 7.4% in early 2026 despite agreed cuts.
frame_summary: The column argues smelting has become a by-product business in which older, disadvantaged plants, many outside China, cannot compete, making the West the likely casualty of China's fight for concentrate.
verbatim_quote: The country’s refined copper output surged by 8% year-on-year to 14.72 million tons in 2025. Global mine production, by contrast, increased by just 1%, according to the International Copper Study Group.
verbatim_list: Annual “benchmark” copper treatment and refining charges (TC/RCs) fell from $80 per metric ton and 8 cents per lb in 2024 to $21.25 and 2.125 cents in 2025. This year they are zero.
But actual production grew by another 7.4% year-on-year between January and April 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

Glencore has already placed its Philippine smelter on care and maintenance and only committed to continue operations at its Australian processing units after receiving an A$600 million ($395 million) bailout from federal and state governments.

Analysts at consultancy CRU estimate that processing fees accounted for 39% of total smelter income in 2018. But last year, the biggest revenue generators were “free metal” and by-product credits, largely for sulfur, at 50-53% and 25-27% respectively.

title: Mount Isa Transformation Study to strengthen local copper
key_claim: A CRU-led consortium began the government-commissioned study of the Mount Isa-Townsville copper value chain, reporting by end-2026, under the Commonwealth-Queensland support package that keeps Glencore's smelter and refinery running.
frame_summary: The trade-press report frames the study as Australia future-proofing sovereign copper processing capability, with the state now underwriting the question of whether the smelter has a commercial future at all.

title: Aurubis delivers improved performance: Increased quarterly result and higher forecast
key_claim: Europe's largest custom smelter raised its full-year forecast to EUR 425-525 million operating EBT, with precious metals, recycling and sulfuric acid revenues more than compensating for considerably lower treatment and refining charges.
frame_summary: Aurubis presents itself as proof that a diversified custom smelter can prosper through the fee collapse, crediting by-products, premiums and recycling rather than concentrate processing income.
